clinicalPearls: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide and in the United States; over half of patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease at diagnosis.

Tobacco smoking accounts for roughly two-thirds of lung cancer deaths globally, but about 65% of new U.S. diagnoses are now in former smokers or never-smokers; one in five women and one in twelve men diagnosed have never smoked.

The WHO divides epithelial lung cancers into four major types: small-cell carcinoma (SCLC) and three non-small-cell types (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large-cell). Together these account for about 90% of epithelial lung cancers; adenocarcinoma is now the most common subtype.

Separating SCLC from NSCLC and, within NSCLC, squamous from nonsquamous histology is essential because natural history and management differ markedly; a generic diagnosis of 'non-small-cell carcinoma, not otherwise specified' is no longer acceptable.

A chronic cough with or without hemoptysis in a current or former smoker with COPD aged 40 or older warrants thorough evaluation for lung cancer even with a normal chest x-ray; a persistent pneumonia unresponsive to repeated antibiotics also requires workup.
Tissue sampling is required to confirm diagnosis in all suspected cases; a core biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration to provide adequate material for molecular and PD-L1 testing.

Central, endobronchial lesions (squamous cell, small-cell, carcinoid) are more readily reached by bronchoscopy, whereas peripheral lesions (adenocarcinoma, large-cell) are more amenable to transthoracic biopsy.
Driver oncogenes (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK, BRAF, MET, HER2, KRAS) are enriched in nonsquamous NSCLC and define distinct molecular cohorts; nearly 90% of SCLCs carry TP53 and RB1 mutations.

Paraneoplastic syndromes are common, especially with SCLC, and may be the presenting feature or first sign of recurrence; they can mimic metastatic disease and lead to inappropriately palliative rather than curative management.
Hypercalcemia from ectopic PTH-related peptide is the most common life-threatening metabolic complication of malignancy and occurs primarily with squamous cell carcinoma.

On FDG PET, a standardized uptake value (SUV) above 2.5 is highly suspicious for malignancy, but PET must never be used alone to diagnose cancer, nodal involvement, or metastasis because of false positives (infection, granulomatous disease such as tuberculosis) and false negatives (lesions under 8 mm, slow-growing tumors, diabetes).

Adenocarcinoma in situ and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (solitary lesions 3 cm or less with pure or predominant lepidic growth and 5 mm or less invasion) achieve near 100% 5-year disease-free survival after complete resection.
harrison.pathophysiology: Inhaled environmental carcinogens, principally those in tobacco smoke, drive transformation of bronchoepithelial cells to a malignant phenotype. Susceptibility is modulated by polymorphisms in carcinogen-metabolizing genes (e.g., CYP1A1) and by genetic loci affecting nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and telomerase (5p15, 6p21, 15q25). Tumorigenesis reflects accumulation of gain-of-function mutations in oncogenes and loss-of-function mutations in tumor-suppressor genes, with the sequence differing by histologic type. Adenocarcinomas frequently harbor targetable driver alterations: activating receptor tyrosine kinase mutations (EGFR, HER2/ERBB2, MET), intracellular signaling mutations (KRAS, BRAF), and chromosomal rearrangements activating ALK, ROS1, RET, and NTRK. Squamous tumors may show FGFR1 amplification, DDR2 mutations, PIK3CA mutations/PTEN loss, and BRAF/MET alterations. Inactivated tumor suppressors include TP53, RB1, RASSF1A, CDKN2A/B, LKB1 (STK11), and FHIT; allelic loss on chromosome 3p occurs very early, even in histologically normal smoke-damaged epithelium. Clinical manifestations arise from central/endobronchial growth (cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, postobstructive pneumonia), peripheral growth (pleural/chest-wall pain, dyspnea, cavitation), regional intrathoracic spread (recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness, phrenic nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, Pancoast syndrome, superior vena cava syndrome, pericardial/lymphatic involvement), distant metastasis, or paraneoplastic mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent or recurrent pneumonia unresponsive to antibiotics
Metastatic carcinoma to the lung from an extrapulmonary primary
Malignant pleural mesothelioma (CK5/6, calretinin, WT-1 positive, distinguishing it from adenocarcinoma)
infectionMimics: Tuberculosis and other granulomatous disease (false-positive FDG-PET uptake; can mimic malignant nodules)
Postobstructive pneumonia from an underlying endobronchial tumor
Parapneumonic pleural effusion mimicking malignant effusion
nonInfectiousMimics: Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes mimicking primary neurologic disease
additionalInvestigations: Chest CT and FDG PET, preferably integrated PET-CT, for anatomic staging and detection of mediastinal nodal and extrathoracic metastases
Tissue biopsy: fiberoptic bronchoscopy with bronchial/transbronchial biopsy, image-guided percutaneous core biopsy, or EBUS-guided biopsy; core biopsy preferred for adequate molecular material
Mediastinal nodal assessment by EBUS- or EUS-guided biopsy, mediastinoscopy, mediastinotomy, thoracoscopy, or thoracotomy
Next-generation sequencing (multigene panel) for driver oncogenes and PD-L1 immunohistochemistry reported as tumor proportion score (TPS)
Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) 'liquid biopsy' when tissue is limited or inaccessible
MRI brain for suspected brain metastases (most effective method) and for superior sulcus tumors to assess brachial plexus involvement

Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 and napsin-A for adenocarcinoma (TTF-1 positive in over 70%, napsin-A in over 90% of primary lung adenocarcinomas), p40/p63 for squamous; neuroendocrine markers (CD56/NCAM, synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1) for SCLC
Thoracentesis with cell block for suspected malignant pleural effusion (repeat if first sample negative)
Spinal CT/MRI for suspected cord compression; brain/spine MRI plus lumbar puncture for suspected leptomeningeal disease
Physiologic evaluation: spirometry (FEV1), DLCO, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (VO2max) before surgical resection
redFlags: Hemoptysis in a smoker over 40 with chronic cough
Hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement) or superior vena cava syndrome
Pancoast/superior sulcus presentation: shoulder pain radiating in ulnar distribution with destruction of first/second ribs, often with Horner syndrome
Signs of cord compression: pain, weakness, paralysis, urinary retention
Weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight (poor prognostic sign)
Hypercalcemia with nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, altered mental status
Symptomatic brain metastases (headache, nausea/vomiting, seizures, focal deficits) or pathologic fractures/bone pain
harrison.prognosis: Outcome is strongly stage-dependent. For NSCLC by the eighth-edition TNM system, 5-year overall survival ranges from roughly 90% for the earliest (stage IA1) disease down to about 10% for stage IVB; SEER data report a 5-year survival of about 63% for localized NSCLC. Lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma has a favorable prognosis, acinar and papillary intermediate, and solid-predominant and micropapillary patterns poor. SCLC is more aggressive: 60-70% present with extensive-stage disease, and even in limited-stage SCLC median survival is roughly 12-20 months historically. Weight loss over 10% of body weight and thrombotic complications of malignancy are poor prognostic signs. Extrathoracic metastases are found at autopsy in over 50% of squamous, about 80% of adenocarcinoma/large-cell, and over 95% of SCLC cases.
pitfalls: A normal chest x-ray does not exclude lung cancer in a high-risk symptomatic smoker.
Negative TTF-1 does not exclude a pulmonary primary; TTF-1 is also positive in neuroendocrine and thyroid tumors.

PET-CT cannot establish a tissue diagnosis: false positives occur with tuberculosis/granulomatous and infectious disease and false negatives with sub-8 mm, slow-growing, or carcinoid/well-differentiated tumors.
Paraneoplastic syndromes may be mistaken for metastatic disease, risking inappropriate palliative rather than curative treatment.
A single negative thoracentesis does not exclude a malignant effusion; repeat sampling is essential.
Diagnosing on small biopsy/cytology specimens may blur squamous-versus-nonsquamous distinction; repeat biopsy is advised in advanced disease for adequate molecular and PD-L1 testing.

Low-dose CT screening carries a high false-positive rate (false-positive rate about 96% among positive screens in NLST), with attendant risks of overdiagnosis, unnecessary procedures, and radiation exposure.
harrison.severityClassification: NSCLC is staged with the eighth-edition (2018) TNM system: T1 (3 cm or less; subdivided T1a 1 cm or less, T1b over 1 to 2 cm, T1c over 2 to 3 cm), T2 (over 3 to 5 cm or visceral pleura/main bronchus involvement/atelectasis; T2a over 3 to 4 cm, T2b over 4 to 5 cm), T3 (over 5 to 7 cm or invasion of chest wall/pericardium/phrenic nerve or satellite nodule in same lobe), T4 (over 7 cm or invasion of mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, recurrent laryngeal nerve, esophagus, vertebra, carina, or separate nodule in a different ipsilateral lobe). Nodes: N0 none, N1 ipsilateral peribronchial/hilar/intrapulmonary, N2 ipsilateral mediastinal/subcarinal, N3 contralateral mediastinal/hilar or scalene/supraclavicular. Metastasis: M1a contralateral nodule or pleural/pericardial nodule/malignant effusion, M1b single extrathoracic metastasis, M1c multiple extrathoracic metastases. SCLC is commonly classified by the two-stage Veterans Administration system: limited-stage (confined to ipsilateral hemithorax within a tolerable radiation port) versus extensive-stage (overt metastatic disease). Physiologic operability thresholds: FEV1 over 2 L or over 80% predicted suggests tolerance of pneumonectomy; FEV1 over 1.5 L suggests adequate reserve for lobectomy; VO2max under 15 mL/kg/min predicts higher postoperative risk; contraindications to thoracic surgery include FEV1 under 1 L, resting PCO2 over 45 mmHg, DLCO under 40%, severe pulmonary hypertension, and recent myocardial infarction.
management: Base treatment on histology and stage, distinguishing small-cell from non-small-cell carcinoma and squamous from nonsquamous disease
Offer surgical resection (lobectomy with nodal sampling), often with adjuvant chemotherapy, for early-stage non-small-cell lung cancer
Direct molecularly targeted agents against driver alterations in advanced adenocarcinoma (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, BRAF, MET or NTRK inhibitors) guided by next-generation sequencing
Use immune checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1/PD-L1 blockade), alone or with platinum-based chemotherapy, guided by the PD-L1 tumour proportion score

Treat small-cell and unresectable locally advanced disease with platinum-based chemotherapy and radiotherapy or concurrent chemoradiation, considering prophylactic cranial irradiation in small-cell disease
Provide early palliative care and symptom control, and support smoking cessation
Manage all cases through a thoracic oncology multidisciplinary team with surveillance imaging for recurrence
